title: Research Data and Repositories
answer: FAIR data, metadata and ontologies, federated sharing, institutional knowledge graphs and long-term preservation.

children.name: FAIR Data
children.blurb: FAIR Data describes a set of principles for making research data and other digital objects findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable by both people and machines.

children.name: Metadata and Ontologies
children.blurb: Metadata and ontologies in research data and repositories concern the structured descriptions that make datasets, models, and papers findable, comparable, and reusable.

children.name: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
children.blurb: Federated sharing of sensitive data refers to systems that let institutions keep sensitive datasets within their own infrastructure while still allowing approved researchers to run analyses across them.

children.name: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
children.blurb: An institutional knowledge graph is a structured representation of the entities and relationships that matter to a research organization, such as people, publications, datasets, projects, grants, equipment, and organizational units.

children.name: Long-Term Digital Preservation
children.blurb: Long-term digital preservation in research data and repositories concerns keeping digital objects readable, usable, and authentic beyond the life of the software, hardware, and institutions that created them.

sections.body: Research data and repositories is the practical work of making scientific information findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable. AI is now doing concrete tasks in this field, such as extracting structured claims from papers, linking datasets to publications, generating metadata from file contents, and matching terms across ontologies. It is not a future promise, systems already parse PDFs, label columns in spreadsheets, and suggest dataset descriptions. The site's library holds 10,555 claims extracted from research works, a small but real example of this extraction work. AI also helps build knowledge graphs by identifying entities and relationships in text. These tools reduce manual cataloguing but do not replace human judgement about what a dataset means.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The state of the field is uneven. FAIR data principles are widely agreed but unevenly applied, and many repositories still rely on manual metadata entry. AI can now generate metadata and link terms with reasonable accuracy for common fields like biomedicine, but it struggles with ambiguous or domain-specific language. Federated sharing of sensitive data has working prototypes, yet legal and technical barriers remain high. Institutional knowledge graphs are often incomplete and require ongoing curation. Long-term digital preservation is still mostly a human and institutional problem, not an AI problem, AI can help with format migration and checksum verification but cannot guarantee readability in fifty years. Honest limits include poor performance on low-resource languages, bias in entity linking, and the risk of silently propagating wrong metadata.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The five pages form a chain from raw data to lasting access. A reader would start with FAIR Data to understand the four principles that shape everything else. Metadata and Ontologies then explains the descriptive layer that makes FAIR possible, including how AI generates and aligns terms. Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data addresses the special case where data cannot be centralized, showing how AI supports privacy-preserving queries and distributed analysis. Institutional Knowledge Graphs moves from individual datasets to the connected web of entities inside one organization, where AI helps build and maintain links. Long-Term Digital Preservation closes the loop by asking what happens to all this data decades from now, and what AI can and cannot do to keep it readable. Together they move from principles, to description, to sharing, to connection, to endurance.
